visual_features.color: entirely jet black coat, bare black face, pinkish bare rump in mature individuals
visual_features.body_shape: stocky robust macaque with elongated muzzle, long prominent crest on crown, long tail (kinked)
visual_features.distinctive_marks: long prominent black crest on crown, entirely black bare face, elongated dog-like muzzle, pink ischial callosities
visual_features.texture: short dense black fur, bare facial skin

description: The Celebes Crested Macaque, also known as the crested black macaque or black ape, and locally as 'yaki', is an Old World monkey endemic to the northeastern tip of Sulawesi, Indonesia, and the adjacent islands of Manadotua and Talise. It is the most endangered of the seven macaque species on Sulawesi. These diurnal primates are primarily terrestrial, spending over 60% of their day on the ground foraging and socializing. They are highly frugivorous, with 70% of their diet consisting of fruits (especially figs). They live in multi-male, multi-female groups of 5–75 individuals, with females outnumbering males by about 4:1. The species gained international fame in 2011 from the 'monkey selfie' controversy.
population_estimate: The total population on Sulawesi is estimated at only 4,000–6,000 individuals. An introduced population of up to 100,000 exists on the island of Bacan (Maluku Islands), but its genetic viability is uncertain. Population density has declined from over 300 individuals per km² in 1980 to fewer than 20–60 individuals per km² today.
habitat: Humid, tropical lowland and upland rainforests at moderate elevations of 700–1,100 m above sea level. They prefer closed-canopy forests and are most abundant in protected areas like Tangkoko Batuangus Nature Reserve. They are also found in disturbed and logged forests, grasslands, and agricultural areas (coconut, corn, sugar palm) where forests have been cleared, though these are suboptimal habitats.
threats: Habitat loss from deforestation and agricultural expansion within an already restricted range
Hunted as a pest due to crop-raiding of coconut, corn, and sugar palm
Illegal wildlife trade (listed on CITES Appendix II)
Small and fragmented populations with limited genetic diversity
Low population density even in protected areas
ecosystem_role: As primary frugivores, Celebes Crested Macaques are keystone seed dispersers in Sulawesi's rainforest ecosystems. They consume large quantities of fruit, especially figs, and disperse seeds throughout their home ranges, contributing significantly to forest regeneration and the maintenance of plant biodiversity in one of the world's most important biodiversity hotspots.
human_connection: Locally known as 'yaki', these macaques are culturally significant in North Sulawesi. They are hunted as pests for raiding crops but are also the focus of major conservation efforts including the Macaca Nigra Project (a collaboration between German Primate Centre and Bogor Agricultural Institute) and Selamatkan Yaki ('Save the Yaki'). The species became internationally famous in 2011 when a crested black macaque took a 'selfie' using wildlife photographer David Slater's camera, sparking a landmark copyright case.
what_students_can_do: Learn about the Macaca Nigra Project and Selamatkan Yaki conservation programs
Support habitat protection in Sulawesi's remaining rainforests
Study primatology to contribute to conservation of critically endangered primates
Raise awareness about the impact of deforestation on endemic island species
Promote sustainable tourism practices in Tangkoko Reserve and other protected areas
Understand the ethical and legal issues surrounding wildlife photography
fun_fact: A crested black macaque gained international fame in 2011 when she took a 'selfie' with a photographer's camera, sparking a years-long legal battle over whether animals can own copyright (they cannot)
